title: It’s coming home: Assessing the 2026 seasons for the Grand Tour host nations
content:

It’s coming home: Assessing the 2026 seasons for the Grand Tour host nations

Pro cycling’s three Grand Tours are hallowed ground for the riders of the men’s peloton. With history dating back over a century, these three-week events are exalted above all other stage races as the pinnacle of achievement in the sport, featuring storied climbs and landscapes that serve as a stage to some of its greatest legends.

For France, Italy and Spain, success not only at their home Grand Tours, but throughout the cycling season at the top level, is not just desired but expected. Fans and media alike place a heavy burden on the shoulders of their athletes to maintain the status of the trio of influential European nations. While the sport still has a way to go when it comes to diversity and representation from nations outside of its European heartlands, nations such as Slovenia, Colombia, Great Britain, Denmark, Ecuador and more have joined and even eclipsed France, Italy and Spain in the modern era, competing comfortably alongside and often surpassing riders from the nations that historically dominated the development of the pro cycling calendar at the top level.

The low countries are just as exacting in their drive for success as the Grand Tour home nations, but where France, Italy and Spain have arguably faltered in recent seasons, Belgium and the Netherlands continue to deliver reasons to celebrate for partisan supporters. In 2026, the two cycling strongholds can lay claim to 12 Grand Tour stages (the same as France, Italy and Spain combined, and including nine at the Tour), one Monument win, and two special jerseys courtesy of Remco Evenepoel, who retained his world ITT title along with winning the European Championship road race. Not a bad haul for one season.

When viewed through the lens of history, it’s fair to say none of the three great cycling superpowers that play host to the trio of Grand Tours are at their peak. These three nations developed pro cycling to where it is today, partially because of these races; just as Belgian names are the most numerous when casting your eye down a list of winners at the cobbled Monuments, so the Giro d’Italia, Tour de France and Vuelta a España contain within their list of winners the greatest ever riders from each nation.

What can we surmise from a fascinating 2026 season, if we view the successes and failures of these three nations as a barometer of their relative health in the sport? Which is most likely to continue populating the sport’s history books in the coming years, and which may become a footnote, despite hosting one of the three most important stage races of the year? It’s time to review the season for the Grand Tour home nations to look for answers.

Reasons to be cheerful for the French

The wait for a male French Tour de France winner is one of the most discussed topics in cycling; since Bernard Hinault in 1985, no Frenchman has been able to repeat the feat, despite the near misses of Laurent Fignon and the romanticised expectations for Thomas Voeckler, Romain Bardet, Thibaut Pinot and Julian Alaphilippe.

The Tour is arguably the hardest race to win in pro cycling, the most hotly contested of the three Grand Tours, and the primary goal for the sport’s elite. Even claiming a precious stage win is a tall order given the quality of the start list, so perhaps it’s not surprising that on paper, the French appear to be the biggest losers in 2026 when it comes to success at their home Grand Tour, given the lack of stage wins for the hosts. It’s only the third time in the race’s history that no French rider has won a stage – a concerning statistic in isolation, but there were other reasons to be cheerful. Three French riders finished in the top ten on GC – fourth, fifth and tenth – with the quiet but steady improvement of Lenny Martinez and consistency of Jordan Jegat adding to the remarkable result on debut by Paul Seixas, the man the French are looking to to end their 41 (and counting) years of hurt.

Away from home, two surprise wins at La Vuelta courtesy of Bastien Tronchon and Bryan Coquard and a trio of victories for Paul Magnier at the Giro d’Italia brought France five Grand Tour stage wins in 2026, with Magnier also claiming the ciclamino points jersey, though their GC strength at home could not be replicated (just 11th at the Giro and eighth, 11th and 12th at the Vuelta).

Despite financial issues plaguing many of their domestic teams, the French have raised their game for the fourth consecutive season: the nation notched up 94 victories 2026, including 24 at WorldTour level. Has the French obsession with winning the Tour obscured reality? Putting aside their preoccupation with the La Grande Boucle, success has come across profiles – the nation boasts one of the strongest young sprinters in Paul Magnier; rising talents in the shape of Aubin Sparfel and Antoine L’Hote, and riders who still haven’t approached their full potential, such as Lenny Martinez, Romain Grégoire and Kévin Vauquelin.

Throw in a Monument win and the tour de force that is Paul Seixas in general, and you have a recipe for future success that should have the French faithful rubbing their hands together.

Italy on an even keel

Of the three nations, Italy occupy the middle ground in terms of their scorecard in 2026. A solid performance at their home Grand Tour, with four stage wins from four different riders (Davide Ballerini, Alberto Bettiol, Filippo Ganna and Jonathan Milan), along with a KOM jersey courtesy of Giulio Ciccone, proved the nation is still performing across all different race profiles. There was less to celebrate at the Tour and Vuelta with no Italian stage wins, and modest GC performances (eighth and ninth at the Vuelta and just 14th at the Tour).

Italy scored 16 WorldTour wins in 2026, from a range of sources – they have top sprinters (Jonathan Milan scored over half of their top level victories), one of the world’s best time triallists, and hope for the future at top stage races after a period in the weeds since Vincenzo Nibali’s retirement. Ciccone flew the flag throughout the season, notching up podiums and top tens at a wide range of races including most recently an agonising second place at the European Champs road race; Giulio Pellizzari continued to make steady progress, recording a clutch of victories at lower tier races, and a notable third on GC at Tirreno-Adriatico; and Davide Piganzoli impressed for Visma with a top ten at the Giro as a domestique, a GC win at the Tour de Luxembourg and Italian Classic victory at the Giro dell’Emilia.

They are the nation that has struggled the most in the past 20 years to produce successful GC riders; Antonio Tiberi had a difficult season and Damiano Caruso’s consistency will be missed, though he was unable to recreate the kinds of results he enjoyed at his peak this year. When it comes to the future though, there is cause for optimism. Lorenzo Finn completed a historic hat-trick in the past calendar year, winning the U23 World Road Race aged just 18, then claiming crushing victories at both bellwether events for development riders in 2026 in the Giro NextGen and Tour de l’Avenir. Finn made his elite debut for Italy in Montréal and will step up to Red Bull’s WorldTour team in 2027 with a view to following in the footsteps of Paul Seixas and making an impact in his first year as a pro – possibly head-to-head against the man who he has clashed with throughout their junior careers. Throw in the promising Matteo Scalco who turns pro with XDS Astana in 2027, and Italy can be cautiously optimistic.

Spain still await long-term successors to their golden era

The inspiration for this piece began with a dive into the state of Spanish cycling. The golden era for the nation that began with Miguel Indurain in the 1990s and continued into the 2000s with the likes of Alberto Contador, Carlos Sastre and latterly Alejandro Valverde has tapered into a less fruitful decade, with Spanish victories at WorldTour level declining year-on-year.

Despite this – and here it’s worth noting that Spain has half the number of top-level pros as France and Italy –  when comparing the three Grand Tour host nations, Spain’s 2026 looks like a slam dunk. A GC victory, and on home soil no less – it’s the stuff dreams are made of, and the first time the Spanish fans have been able to celebrate a Vuelta victory since Contador’s final win there in 2014.

The Spanish have won just six WorldTour races in 2026, including just a single Grand Tour stage – Igor Arrieta’s scintillating breakaway victory at the Giro d’Italia. It’s approaching a decade since their last Monument win, and with their best-placed riders on GC at the Giro and Tour 14th and seventh respectively (David de la Cruz at the Giro and Juan Ayuso at the Tour), the state of play appears comparatively bleak for the nation, which, on paper, enjoyed the best of 2026 in Grand Tour terms. Enric Mas’s surprise Vuelta victory combined with stage wins along the way for both Mas and a revitalised Mikel Landa offered respite for the languishing Spanish, Mas discovering form that saw him become one of a handful of riders to be able to match Tadej Pogačar; but taking nothing away from his deserved victory, it’s fair to say both he and particularly Landa are heading towards the twilight of their careers.

As for the future, there are a host of young Spanish talents rising through the ranks that will hope to compete with the likes of Seixas and Finn. Among them, Lidl-Trek’s Héctor Álvarez, who has scorched his way through his second year at U23, taking victory most recently at the European Championships. The same year group as the French and Italian hopes, Álvarez has a slightly different profile to the two climbers, more likely destined for Classics success than three-week stage races.

Add in Netcompany Ineos-bound Junior World Road and Time-Trial Champion Benjamin Noval, whose new team and home nation are hoping he can be a Seixas-like figure, and there is real cause for hope in Spain’s future. Both join Seixas and Finn as WorldTour pros in 2027, and alongside the likes of Pau Marti, Iván Romeo and Markel Beloki – who’ll join Noval at Netcompany – will look to kickstart a new era of Spanish success, hot on the heels of Juan Ayuso, who himself will hope to rediscover his best level after a faltering first season with Lidl-Trek.

Tangible routes to glory

All three nations had reasons to celebrate in 2026, but though Spain arguably came out on top with a Grand Tour GC win, France can perhaps feel the greatest sense of optimism, particularly given the way their season has ended with a first career Monument win for Paul Seixas – a confirmation of the prodigiously talented 20-year-old’s vast potential. His impressive fourth place in his Tour de France debut strikes an ominous note for the other cycling superpowers too, who will hope their young talents can eventually be a match for the rising French star, otherwise the French may finally be able to reclaim their dominance at not only their home Grand Tour, but across cycling.

Italy and Spain have their own Seixas-esque figures, but as far as future-proofing goes, France finally has the most tangible route to victory already mobilised and ready to deliver the glory they’ve been so craving.
